title: Intersection of Two Arrays
description: Find the unique values present in both of two arrays, using a hash set for O(1) membership checks.

blocks.text: Given two integer arrays nums1 and nums2, return an array of their intersection. Each element in the result must be unique. Since the original problem allows any order, this document produces a sorted-ascending result for a deterministic, verifiable output.

blocks.caption: A hash set of one array lets the other array be scanned for shared values in linear time.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums1[], nums2[] (can contain duplicates within each array)"],["Output","Unique values present in BOTH arrays"],["Order","Any order accepted by the original problem; this document uses sorted-ascending for determinism"]]}

blocks.text: "Which elements appear in both collections" is a classic hash-set membership problem: put one array into a set for O(1) lookups, then scan the other array checking membership.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This is the array-intersection sibling of the far more common "does this element exist" hash-set pattern seen throughout the Hash Tables category.

Picture two guest lists for different events. The "common guests" list should contain every name that appears on BOTH lists, with each name listed only once even if it appeared multiple times on either original list.

blocks.caption: A name only makes the common list if it appears in both original lists, listed once.

items: Put every value from nums1 into a hash set for O(1) membership checks.
Scan nums2, adding any value found in that set to a RESULT set (which naturally deduplicates).
Sort the final result for a single, deterministic, verifiable output.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The result set contains {4, 9}. Sorted ascending, the deterministic output is [4, 9], matching what this document's algorithm produces exactly.
A direct approach checks every element of nums1 against every element of nums2, which is correct but quadratic in the worst case.
Converting one array to a hash set turns each membership check into O(1), so scanning the other array once finds all shared values in linear time overall.
For each value in nums1, scan all of nums2 looking for a match, adding matches to a result set.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n * m)","n and m are the lengths of nums1 and nums2, every pair checked"],["Space","O(min(n, m))","The result set, at most the smaller array's unique count"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Repeatedly rescanning nums2 for every element of nums1 is unnecessary once membership can be checked in O(1) via a hash set.
Build a hash set from nums1 once, O(n). Then scan nums2 once, adding any value found in that set to a result set, O(m). Sort the result for a deterministic output.

items: Scan nums2, checking membership in set1 and collecting matches into a result set, O(m).
Sort the result set for a single canonical output.

items: Converting one collection to a hash set is the standard way to speed up repeated membership checks from O(n) to O(1) each.
Using a set (not a list) for the result naturally deduplicates without extra bookkeeping.
Sorting is a simple, common way to produce a single deterministic answer when a problem otherwise accepts any order.

blocks.text: Intersection of Two Arrays is solved by converting one array to a hash set for O(1) membership checks, then scanning the other array once to collect shared values into a deduplicated result set. Sorting that result gives a single deterministic output in O(n + m) time.
